Antipatris
an-TIP-ah-tris
proper noun
Greek Antipatris, a town on the road from Jerusalem to Caesarea, rebuilt by Herod the Great and named in honour of his father Antipater.

📖 Biblical Definition

Antipatris was a town upon the great road running down from Jerusalem to Caesarea by the sea, rebuilt by Herod the Great and named for his father Antipater. It enters Scripture at a single verse, yet a memorable one, for it was the night station of a Roman escort guarding the apostle Paul: “Then the soldiers, as it was commanded them, took Paul, and brought him by night to Antipatris” (Act 23:31). Forty Jewish assassins had bound themselves under a curse to kill him, but the plot was uncovered by a young kinsman, and the chief captain sent Paul away under cover of darkness with a great guard of horsemen and footmen. The whole march to Antipatris preaches the providence of God, who set a hedge of Roman spears about His servant that not one hair of his head should fall until his appointed work was done. The Lord had already stood by Paul the night before and said, “so must thou bear witness also at Rome”; and no ambush of forty men, no oath, no darkness could hinder that word. He who made of one blood all nations and “determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation” (Act 17:26) was directing every mile of that midnight ride. The heathen were promised for Christ’s inheritance and “the uttermost parts of the earth” for His possession (Psa 2:8); and to carry that gospel to Rome, God moved a garrison to guard one chained preacher.

📜 Webster 1828 Definition

A town on the Jerusalem-to-Caesarea road whither soldiers brought Paul by night, guarding him from ambush (Act 23:31); a witness to the providence that keeps God’s servant for his appointed work.

ANTIPATRIS, a town on the road from Jerusalem to Caesarea (Act 23:31).

Rebuilt by Herod the Great and named for his father Antipater.

The night station of the Roman guard escorting Paul from ambush.

Forty men had sworn to kill him; the plot was uncovered and foiled.

A witness to the providence that guards God’s servant to bear witness at Rome.

📖 Key Scripture

Act 23:31 — "Then the soldiers, as it was commanded them, took Paul, and brought him by night to Antipatris."

Act 17:26 — "And hath made of one blood all nations of men for to dwell on all the face of the earth, and hath determined the times before appointed, and the bounds of their habitation;"

Psa 2:8 — "Ask of me, and I shall give thee the heathen for thine inheritance, and the uttermost parts of the earth for thy possession."

Mal 1:11 — "For from the rising of the sun even unto the going down of the same my name shall be great among the Gentiles; and in every place incense shall be offered unto my name, and a pure offering: for my name shall be great among the heathen, saith the LORD of hosts."

⚠️ Modern Corruption

The night station whither Paul was borne under guard; the entry recovers the providence that hedges God’s servant about until his appointed testimony is finished.

expand to see more

Antipatris is a plain waypoint on the coastal road, a Herodian town named for Antipater; the place bears no modern controversy, only the memory of a midnight march that saved an apostle’s life.

This entry faces no significant postmodern redefinition. The principle to recover is the particular providence of God over His servants. Forty men had sworn Paul’s death, yet the plot was uncovered by a boy and foiled by a garrison, and the apostle was borne safely by night to Antipatris. The Lord had said he must bear witness at Rome, and no oath or ambush could break that word. God, who fixed the bounds of the nations’ habitation, moved Roman spears to guard one chained preacher until his testimony was done.

🔗 Greek & Hebrew Roots

Greek Antipatris, a place-name honouring Antipater, father of Herod the Great, formed with the possessive suffix marking a city.

expand to see more

Antipatris — Greek Antipatris, named for Antipater (Act 23:31).

Antipater was the father of Herod the Great.

The town lay on the road from Jerusalem down to Caesarea.

Rebuilt by Herod upon an older site in the plain of Sharon.

A one-verse waypoint, yet a monument of providence.

Usage

"The soldiers brought Paul by night to Antipatris."

"Antipatris lay on the road down to Caesarea by the sea."

"At Antipatris the mounted escort turned back, the danger past."
